definition: In this historical mind-body view, mental and bodily events are understood as the same underlying reality described in two different ways. Rather than treating mind and body as causing one another, it presents them as parallel aspects or manifestations of a single unity.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Double Aspect Theory; pinned source text

reasons: The packet supports Double Aspect Theory / psychophysical parallelism, not identity theory as the primary term; it only mentions “the identity theory of mind and body” in passing and does not establish identity theory as the sense to define.

The definition compresses the doctrine into a modern-sounding identity view; the source emphasizes parallelism/concomitance and explicitly denies causal interaction, rather than simply equating mind and body in the way the term “identity theory” suggests.

The packet does not provide a standalone definition of “identity theory” as a term; it only notes that the German “psychophysischer Parallelismus” is “not an adequate equivalent, unless connected with the identity theory of mind and body,” without defining identity theory itself.

Because the packet never explicitly states that “identity theory” means the “double aspect/single unity with parallel mind and body” position, the provided definition risks assigning the requested sense of “identity theory” without direct support from the packet.
